title: Design a Maps & Routing System (Google Maps)
prompt: Design the routing and maps backend behind a service like Google Maps: render the map, and compute the fastest route between two points on a continent-scale road network with live traffic, returning a route and ETA in well under a second. Cover map tile serving, the routing engine, and how traffic and ETAs stay fresh.
blurb: The continent-scale shortest-path problem — why plain Dijkstra can't answer in time, graph preprocessing (contraction hierarchies), tiled map rendering, and traffic-aware ETAs.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (map rendering, point-to-point routing, ETA, alternatives, turn-by-turn, live traffic) from non-functional (sub-second routing, freshness of traffic, availability, global scale).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about scale (graph size, QPS), latency target, modes (drive/walk/transit), how fresh traffic must be, static vs dynamic routing.

rubric.label: Map tile serving
rubric.description: Pre-rendered vs vector tiles, zoom-level pyramid, tile keys, aggressive CDN caching, why rendering is a separate read-heavy problem from routing.

rubric.label: Road-network graph model
rubric.description: Modeling roads as a weighted directed graph (nodes=intersections, edges=segments), turn restrictions, edge weights as travel time, storage of a continent-scale graph.

rubric.label: Routing algorithm depth
rubric.description: Why plain Dijkstra/A* is too slow at continent scale; preprocessing techniques (contraction hierarchies, ALT, arc-flags, hub labeling) enabling millisecond queries; A* with good heuristics.

rubric.label: Partitioning & scale
rubric.description: Partitioning the graph into regions/tiles, hierarchical routing (local + highway networks), sharding preprocessed data, handling cross-partition long routes.

rubric.label: ETA & live traffic
rubric.description: Edge weights from historical + live speeds, ingesting GPS probe data, updating weights without full re-preprocessing, ML/time-dependent ETA, dynamic re-routing.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Client -> tile service (CDN) for rendering + routing service (preprocessed graph) + traffic pipeline updating weights; ETA service.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: CDN for tiles, replicating/sharding the preprocessed graph in memory, caching popular routes/corridors, batching traffic updates.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: Preprocessing cost vs freshness (re-CH on traffic change), long cross-region queries, tile hotspots, traffic-ingest volume.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Route latency, ETA accuracy vs actual, traffic-pipeline lag, tile cache hit ratio, re-route rates.

functional_requirements: Render the map at multiple zoom levels
Compute the fastest route between two points
Incorporate live traffic into routes and ETAs
nonfunctional_requirements: Route + ETA returned in well under a second
Map tiles served with very high cache hit ratio
ETA accuracy close to real travel time
clarifying_questions: Continent/global graph size (nodes/edges) and routing QPS?
Latency target for a route request?
Which modes — driving, walking, cycling, transit?
How fresh must live traffic be, and do we have GPS probe data?
Do we need alternatives, and dynamic re-routing during navigation?
Is turn-by-turn (voice/instructions) in scope, or just route + ETA?
qualifying_questions: Is preprocessing latency (rebuild on traffic change) an acceptable tradeoff for fast queries?
How large is the probe-data firehose we must ingest?

estimations.graph: A continent road graph is tens of millions of nodes and ~100M+ edges — too big to Dijkstra per request within budget; must preprocess.
estimations.dijkstra_cost: Plain Dijkstra over 10s of millions of nodes visits a huge fraction of the graph — hundreds of ms to seconds. Contraction hierarchies answer the same query in ~sub-millisecond after preprocessing.
estimations.tiles: Zoom pyramid: level z has 4^z tiles; global coverage to high zoom is billions of tiles — pre-render popular areas, cache hard at the CDN (hit ratio >95%).
estimations.traffic: Millions of GPS probes/sec aggregate into per-edge speed estimates; update weights incrementally rather than re-preprocessing the whole graph.

core_components: Routing service (holds preprocessed graph in memory)
data_model: graph: nodes(intersection id, lat, lng), edges(from, to, length, base_time, road_class, turn_restrictions)
ch_data: contraction shortcuts + node ordering per partition
tiles(z, x, y, rendered_blob / vector data)
probes(anonymized speed samples) -> aggregated per edge
api_design: GET /eta?route -> updated ETA with live traffic
POST /reroute { current_pos, dest } -> new route during navigation
reference.high_level_design: Map rendering and routing are two separate problems. Tiles are pre-rendered (or vector tiles rendered client-side) into a z/x/y pyramid and served overwhelmingly from a CDN — this read-heavy path is cache-dominated. Routing runs on a routing service that holds a preprocessed road graph in memory. Because plain Dijkstra/A* is too slow on a continent-scale graph, an offline pipeline preprocesses the graph (e.g. contraction hierarchies) so a query only touches a tiny 'highway' of shortcut edges and returns in sub-millisecond; A* with landmark (ALT) heuristics is an alternative. Edge weights encode travel time, blending historical time-of-day speed profiles with live traffic. A traffic pipeline ingests anonymized GPS probes, aggregates per-edge live speeds, and updates weights incrementally; because full CH re-preprocessing is expensive, live traffic is applied via customizable/partition-level updates rather than rebuilding the whole hierarchy. The graph is partitioned into regions so preprocessing and updates are local, with hierarchical routing stitching long cross-region trips via the highway network. An ETA service and dynamic re-routing use the same weights.

deep_dives.probe: Plain Dijkstra on 50M nodes won't hit your latency budget. Explain how contraction hierarchies (or ALT/arc-flags/hub-labeling) preprocess the graph so queries become near-instant, and what preprocessing costs you.

How do live-traffic edge-weight changes get into routing without re-running full CH preprocessing on the whole continent? (customizable CH / partition-local updates / overlay.) How do historical profiles and live speeds combine into an ETA?
How do you partition a continent graph, and how does a route from one region to a far region get computed — hierarchical/overlay routing across partitions?
Why serve map rendering as tiles through a CDN separate from routing? Vector vs raster tiles, the zoom pyramid, and how you keep the cache hit ratio very high.
During turn-by-turn, the driver misses a turn or traffic changes. How do you detect it and re-route quickly using the already-loaded graph?

Aggregated edge speeds and map/road updates live in datastores, and multiple systems (routing nodes, ETA, analytics) must pick up changes promptly. How do you propagate these — change data capture / a change stream off the store, or dual writes — and how do you push fresh weights to in-memory routing replicas without a stampede?

scaling: CDN + zoom pyramid for tiles (cache-dominated read path)
Replicate the preprocessed graph in memory across routing nodes; shard by region
Cache popular routes/corridors and common OD pairs
Batch and incrementally apply traffic updates rather than full re-preprocessing
Hierarchical routing to keep cross-region queries cheap
bottlenecks: Preprocessing cost vs traffic freshness (rebuild latency)
Tile hotspots / cache invalidation on map updates
GPS probe ingest volume and per-edge aggregation
tradeoffs: Contraction hierarchies (fast queries, costly/slow to rebuild) vs plain Dijkstra/A* (no preprocessing, slow queries)
Customizable CH / overlays (cheap traffic updates) vs full CH (best query speed, expensive updates)
Pre-rendered raster tiles (simple, storage-heavy) vs vector tiles (flexible, client renders)
Fresher traffic (more re-weighting cost) vs cheaper compute (staler ETAs)
alternative_solutions: Contraction Hierarchies (with Customizable CH for live traffic)
ALT (A* + landmarks) for lower preprocessing cost
Arc-flags / hub-labeling for very fast queries
Time-dependent / ML ETA models layered over the base route
observability: Route query latency (p99) and preprocessing/update lag
ETA accuracy vs actual travel time
Tile CDN hit ratio and origin load
Re-route frequency and cross-region query share
security: Rate-limit routing/tile APIs and abuse detection
Authn for personalized/history features; minimize retained location data
Protect against scraping of the full graph / tiles
reference.reference_answer: A staff-level answer splits the problem: map rendering is a read-heavy tiled CDN problem (zoom pyramid, vector/raster tiles, high cache hit ratio) while routing is a graph problem. It models roads as a weighted directed graph with turn restrictions and recognizes that plain Dijkstra/A* cannot meet a sub-second budget at continent scale, so it preprocesses with contraction hierarchies (or ALT/arc-flags/hub-labeling) for near-instant queries, held in memory and sharded by region with hierarchical/overlay routing for long trips. It builds edge weights from historical time-of-day profiles plus live traffic ingested from anonymized GPS probes, applying updates incrementally (customizable CH / partition-local) rather than re-preprocessing the continent, and layers an ETA model. It caches popular corridors, propagates speed/map updates to routing replicas via CDC/change streams without stampede, and names preprocessing-vs-freshness and cross-region queries as the key bottlenecks.

interviewer_notes: The defining moment is when the candidate confronts that Dijkstra/A* on a continent graph can't answer in time and reaches for graph preprocessing (contraction hierarchies, ALT, arc-flags, hub-labeling) — push hard here; naming a technique and its preprocessing-vs-query-speed tradeoff is the staff signal. Make sure they separate tiled map rendering (CDN, read-heavy) from routing. The second hard problem is live traffic: applying weight changes without full re-preprocessing (customizable CH / overlays) and blending historical + live speeds into an ETA. If they mention tiles/CDN/cache, probe invalidation and stampede on map version bumps; if they mention a datastore for speeds/map, hit the CDC/change-stream probe plus refreshing in-memory graph replicas without a herd. Cover partitioning and cross-region routing if time allows.
